from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout(
            "The Magic of the Central Limit Theorem: Order from Chaos",
            [
                "Welcome to the mysterious forest of unpredictable monsters.",
                "Monster heights here follow a messy, chaotic distribution.",
                "Some are tiny squirrels, others are giant redwood trees.",
                "Meet Zog, a scientist trying to find the average.",
                "Can we find order in this wild, random data?"
            ]
        )

        # Colors for reference
        MONSTER_COLORS = ["#FF5733", "#33FF57", "#3357FF", "#F333FF", "#FFFF33", 
                          "#33FFFF", "#FF3357", "#57FF33", "#5733FF", "#FF8C00"]
        CHART_COLOR = "#808080"
        HIGHLIGHT_COLOR = "#FFFF00"
        ZOG_COLOR = "#FFFFFF"
        QUESTION_COLOR = "#00FFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        
        monsters = VGroup()
        heights = [0.6, 0.4, 0.8, 0.7, 0.2, 0.9, 0.5, 0.6, 1.1, 2.0]
        positions = ['A1', 'A2', 'A3', 'B1', 'B2', 'B3', 'B4', 'C1', 'C2', 'D5']
        
        for h, pos, col in zip(heights, positions, MONSTER_COLORS):
            m = Rectangle(height=h, width=0.3, fill_opacity=0.8, color=col)
            self.place_at_grid(m, pos)
            monsters.add(m)
            
        self.play(FadeIn(monsters))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(GRAY),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(CHART_COLOR)
        )
        
        chart_bars = VGroup()
        for i in range(12):
            h = np.random.uniform(0.3, 1.2)
            b = Rectangle(height=h, width=0.15, fill_opacity=0.6, color=CHART_COLOR)
            chart_bars.add(b)
        chart_bars.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        self.place_in_area(chart_bars, 'E1', 'F6')
        
        self.play(Create(chart_bars))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(GRAY),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(HIGHLIGHT_COLOR)
        )
        
        circle_tiny = Circle(radius=0.2, color=HIGHLIGHT_COLOR).move_to(self.grid['B2'])
        circle_giant = Circle(radius=0.6, color=HIGHLIGHT_COLOR).move_to(self.grid['D5'])
        
        self.play(Create(circle_tiny), Create(circle_giant))
        self.play(circle_tiny.animate.scale(1.2), circle_giant.animate.scale(1.1), rate_func=there_and_back)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(GRAY),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(ZOG_COLOR)
        )
        
        zog_body = Circle(radius=0.25, color=ZOG_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.2)
        glass_l = Circle(radius=0.06, color=ZOG_COLOR).shift(LEFT*0.08 + UP*0.04)
        glass_r = Circle(radius=0.06, color=ZOG_COLOR).shift(RIGHT*0.08 + UP*0.04)
        bridge = Line(glass_l.get_right(), glass_r.get_left(), color=ZOG_COLOR)
        zog_face = VGroup(zog_body, glass_l, glass_r, bridge)
        zog_label = Text("Zog", font_size=18, color=ZOG_COLOR).next_to(zog_body, DOWN, buff=0.1)
        zog_group = VGroup(zog_face, zog_label)
        self.place_at_grid(zog_group, 'C6')
        
        self.play(FadeIn(zog_group))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(GRAY),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(QUESTION_COLOR)
        )
        
        q_mark = MathTex("?", color=QUESTION_COLOR).scale(3)
        self.place_in_area(q_mark, 'C3', 'C4')
        
        # Pulse animation setup
        pulse_tracker = ValueTracker(1.0)
        q_mark.add_updater(lambda m: m.scale(pulse_tracker.get_value() / m.get_height() * 2.0)) # Simplified scaling

        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(chart_bars, q_mark),
            FadeOut(monsters),
            FadeOut(circle_tiny),
            FadeOut(circle_giant)
        )
        
        # Pulse effect
        self.play(pulse_tracker.animate.set_value(1.2), run_time=0.5, rate_func=there_and_back)
        self.play(pulse_tracker.animate.set_value(1.2), run_time=0.5, rate_func=there_and_back)
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Set seed for reproducible monster scatter
        np.random.seed(42)
        
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite Knowledge: Populations vs. Samples", [
            "The entire forest population has a mean and spread.",
            "Zog captures a small random group called a sample.",
            "This sample's average height is the sample mean."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Color change for the current lecture line
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Monsters (forest population) represented by small circular blobs
        monsters = VGroup(*[
            Circle(radius=0.07, color=GREEN_D, fill_opacity=0.7, stroke_width=1) 
            for _ in range(40)
        ])
        
        # Scatter monsters randomly within the forest area (A1 to F6)
        # Forest bounds roughly: X [0.6, 5.4], Y [-2.7, 2.1]
        for m in monsters:
            m.move_to([
                np.random.uniform(0.7, 5.3),
                np.random.uniform(-2.6, 2.0),
                0
            ])

        # Rectangle representing the forest area / Population
        pop_rect = Rectangle(width=5.2, height=5.2, color=GREY_A).set_stroke(opacity=0.3)
        self.place_in_area(pop_rect, "A1", "F6")
        
        pop_label = Text("Population (N)", font_size=24, color=YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "A1", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Mean (mu) and Spread (sigma) symbols
        mu_sym = MathTex("\\mu", color=YELLOW, font_size=44)
        sigma_sym = MathTex("\\sigma", color=YELLOW, font_size=44)
        self.place_at_grid(mu_sym, "A5")
        self.place_at_grid(sigma_sym, "A6")
        
        self.play(
            FadeIn(monsters),
            Create(pop_rect),
            Write(pop_label),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.play(Write(mu_sym), Write(sigma_sym))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Reset previous color, highlight current line
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(BLUE)
        
        # Define a 'Net' for the sample
        net = Circle(radius=0.75, color=BLUE, stroke_width=4)
        self.place_in_area(net, "C3", "D4") 
        
        sample_label = Text("Sample (n=5)", font_size=24, color=BLUE)
        self.place_at_grid(sample_label, "B2", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Pick 5 random monsters to move into the net
        # We use a fixed subset for consistency
        sample_indices = [3, 8, 15, 22, 35]
        sample_group = VGroup(*[monsters[i] for i in sample_indices])
        
        sample_move_anims = []
        for i, m in enumerate(sample_group):
            # Radial arrangement inside the net
            angle = i * (2 * PI / 5)
            offset = np.array([0.35 * np.cos(angle), 0.35 * np.sin(angle), 0])
            sample_move_anims.append(m.animate.move_to(net.get_center() + offset).set_color(BLUE))
            
        self.play(
            Create(net),
            Write(sample_label),
            *sample_move_anims,
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Reset previous color, highlight current line
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(ORANGE)
        
        # Sample Mean (x-bar) symbol
        x_bar_sym = MathTex("\\bar{x}", color=ORANGE, font_size=44)
        self.place_at_grid(x_bar_sym, "F6")
        
        # Flash symbols to connect lecture concepts
        self.play(
            Indicate(mu_sym, color=YELLOW, scale_factor=1.2),
            Write(x_bar_sym)
        )
        self.play(Indicate(x_bar_sym, color=ORANGE, scale_factor=1.2))
        
        self.wait(3)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout(
            "The Experiment: The Power of Repetition",
            [
                "We repeat this sampling process thousands of times.",
                "Each group's average is recorded as a single data point.",
                "A collection of these averages forms a new distribution."
            ]
        )
        
        # Colors for lecture lines
        colors = [TEAL, YELLOW, ORANGE]

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "We repeat this sampling process thousands of times."
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(colors[0]))

        # Visual: Conveyor belt carrying 'Groups of 30' monsters
        belt = Line(self.grid["B1"] + LEFT*0.5, self.grid["B6"] + RIGHT*0.5, color=GREY_B)
        belt_label = Text("Conveyor Belt", font_size=16, color=GREY_B)
        self.place_at_grid(belt_label, "A1", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        # Create a "Group of 30" representation
        def create_monster_group():
            monsters = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.05, color=BLUE) for _ in range(15)])
            monsters.arrange_in_grid(rows=3, cols=5, buff=0.05)
            label = Text("n=30", font_size=14, color=BLUE).next_to(monsters, UP, buff=0.1)
            return VGroup(monsters, label)

        group1 = create_monster_group()
        group2 = create_monster_group()
        
        self.place_at_grid(group1, "B1")
        self.place_at_grid(group2, "B1")
        group2.shift(LEFT * 2)

        self.add(belt, belt_label)
        
        # Animate movement
        moving_groups = VGroup(group1, group2)
        self.play(
            moving_groups.animate.shift(RIGHT * 3),
            run_time=2,
            rate_func=linear
        )
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # "Each group's average is recorded as a single data point."
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(colors[1]))

        # Number line at the bottom
        number_line = NumberLine(
            x_range=[0, 10, 1],
            length=5,
            include_numbers=True,
            font_size=16,
            color=WHITE
        )
        self.place_in_area(number_line, "F1", "F6")
        nl_label = Text("Distribution of Means", font_size=16, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(nl_label, "E6", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.add(number_line, nl_label)

        # For the first group, drop a mean dot
        mean_dot = Dot(color=colors[1], radius=0.08)
        # Position it where group1 is currently (roughly B4)
        mean_dot.move_to(group1.get_center())
        
        # Drop to the number line
        target_pos = number_line.n2p(5) # Arbitrary mean value
        self.play(
            FadeIn(mean_dot),
            mean_dot.animate.move_to(target_pos),
            run_time=1
        )
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # "A collection of these averages forms a new distribution."
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(colors[2]))

        # Rapidly repeat dot dropping
        # We'll simulate many dots dropping to form stacks
        
        # Function to drop a dot to a specific value
        def get_drop_animation(value, offset_y=0):
            d = Dot(color=colors[2], radius=0.06)
            # Start from belt height
            start_pos = self.grid["B3"]
            d.move_to(start_pos)
            target = number_line.n2p(val) + UP * offset_y
            return FadeIn(d), d.animate.move_to(target)

        # Create a set of "samples"
        sample_values = [4, 6, 5, 5, 4, 6, 7, 3, 5, 5, 6, 4, 5]
        stacks = {v: 0 for v in set(sample_values)}
        
        animations = []
        for val in sample_values:
            fade_in, move = get_drop_animation(val, offset_y=stacks[val]*0.12)
            animations.append(fade_in)
            animations.append(move)
            stacks[val] += 1

        # Play animations in batches to look "rapid"
        self.play(AnimationGroup(*animations[:8], lag_ratio=0.1))
        self.play(AnimationGroup(*animations[8:16], lag_ratio=0.1))
        self.play(AnimationGroup(*animations[16:], lag_ratio=0.1))

        self.wait(2)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout(
            "The Core Revelation: The Bell Curve Emerges",
            [
                "Watch as the collection of averages begins to change.",
                "The chaotic forest data transforms into a symmetrical shape.",
                "A perfect bell curve emerges from the underlying chaos.",
                "This magic happens regardless of the original distribution's shape.",
                "With enough samples, the Central Limit Theorem always wins."
            ]
        )

        # Colors
        COLOR_FOREST = "#888888" # Grey for "chaos"
        COLOR_MEAN = "#3498DB"   # Blue for sample means
        COLOR_BELL = "#00FF00"   # Green for the bell curve
        COLOR_TEXT = "#F1C40F"   # Yellow/Gold for the condition

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # 1. Forest Distribution Chart (Chaotic/Bimodal)
        forest_axes = Axes(
            x_range=[0, 10, 2], y_range=[0, 1, 0.2],
            x_length=2.5, y_length=2,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "font_size": 14}
        ).set_color(GRAY_C)
        forest_label = Text("Forest Dist.", font_size=18, color=GRAY_A)
        forest_group = VGroup(forest_axes, forest_label).arrange(DOWN, buff=0.1)
        
        # Bimodal "messy" distribution
        forest_dist = forest_axes.plot(
            lambda x: 0.4 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x - 2)**2) + 0.6 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x - 7)**2),
            color=COLOR_FOREST
        )
        self.place_in_area(forest_group, 'A1', 'C3', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.add(forest_group, forest_dist)

        # 2. Sample Mean Distribution Chart (Starts empty)
        mean_axes = Axes(
            x_range=[0, 10, 2], y_range=[0, 1, 0.2],
            x_length=2.5, y_length=2,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "font_size": 14}
        ).set_color(GRAY_C)
        mean_label = Text("Sample Mean Dist.", font_size=18, color=COLOR_MEAN)
        mean_group = VGroup(mean_axes, mean_label).arrange(DOWN, buff=0.1)
        
        self.place_in_area(mean_group, 'A4', 'C6', scale_factor=1.0)
        self.play(Create(mean_axes), Write(mean_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_MEAN)
        
        # Histogram bars representing "filling dots"
        # We will simulate the growth of bars into a bell shape
        num_bars = 15
        bar_x_positions = np.linspace(2, 8, num_bars)
        
        # Normal distribution values for final state
        def normal_pdf(x, mu=5, sigma=1.2):
            return 0.8 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sigma)**2)

        bars = VGroup(*[
            Rectangle(
                width=2.5/num_bars, 
                height=0.01, 
                fill_color=COLOR_MEAN, 
                fill_opacity=0.7, 
                stroke_width=1
            ).move_to(mean_axes.c2p(x, 0), aligned_edge=DOWN)
            for x in bar_x_positions
        ])
        
        self.add(bars)
        
        # Growth animation (Simulating 1,000 dots)
        growth_anims = []
        for i, bar in enumerate(bars):
            target_height = normal_pdf(bar_x_positions[i])
            growth_anims.append(bar.animate.stretch_to_fit_height(
                mean_axes.get_y_unit_size() * target_height, about_edge=DOWN
            ))
            
        self.play(AnimationGroup(*growth_anims, lag_ratio=0.05), run_time=3)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_BELL)
        
        # Overlay a smooth green curve
        bell_curve = mean_axes.plot(
            lambda x: normal_pdf(x),
            color=COLOR_BELL,
            stroke_width=4
        )
        
        self.play(Create(bell_curve))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(LIGHT_PINK)
        
        # To show it works regardless of shape, we flash a uniform and exponential shape briefly
        uniform_dist = forest_axes.plot(lambda x: 0.5 if 2 < x < 8 else 0, color=LIGHT_PINK)
        exp_dist = forest_axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x/2) if x > 0 else 0, color=LIGHT_PINK)
        
        self.play(Transform(forest_dist, uniform_dist))
        self.wait(0.5)
        self.play(Transform(forest_dist, exp_dist))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color(COLOR_TEXT)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # 1. Setup Layout
        title_text = "The Mathematical Logic: Mean and Spread"
        lecture_lines = [
            "The bell curve centers exactly at the population mean.",
            "Increasing sample size makes the bell curve much narrower.",
            "Larger samples provide a more precise estimate of truth.",
            "This relationship follows the predictable Standard Error formula.",
            "Precision grows as the square root of sample size."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Apply color changes to lecture lines for visual association
        line_colors = [WHITE, "#FF00FF", "#00FFFF", "#FFFF00", "#FFFF00"]
        for i, color in enumerate(line_colors):
            self.lecture[i].set_color(color)

        # Helper function for bell curves (Normal Distribution)
        def get_bell_curve(sigma, color):
            return FunctionGraph(
                lambda x: np.exp(-0.5 * (x / sigma)**2) / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)),
                x_range=[-3.0, 3.0],
                color=color
            )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "The bell curve centers exactly at the population mean."
        mu_line = Line(start=DOWN * 1.5, end=UP * 2.0, color=WHITE, stroke_width=2)
        mu_label = MathTex(r"\mu", color=WHITE)
        
        # Position mean line at E4
        self.place_at_grid(mu_line, "E4")
        mu_label.next_to(mu_line, UP, buff=0.1)
        
        # Background wide curve (faded) to represent the initial distribution
        curve_wide = get_bell_curve(1.2, "#FF00FF")
        self.place_at_grid(curve_wide, "E4")
        curve_wide.set_stroke(opacity=0.3)

        self.play(Create(curve_wide))
        self.play(Create(mu_line), Write(mu_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # "Increasing sample size makes the bell curve much narrower."
        label_small = Text("Small Sample (n=5)", font_size=20, color="#FF00FF")
        self.place_at_grid(label_small, "B2")
        
        self.play(
            curve_wide.animate.set_stroke(opacity=1.0),
            Write(label_small)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # "Larger samples provide a more precise estimate of truth."
        # Transitioning to a narrower distribution (Large n)
        curve_narrow = get_bell_curve(0.5, "#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(curve_narrow, "E4")
        
        label_large = Text("Large Sample (n=100)", font_size=20, color="#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(label_large, "B6")
        
        self.play(
            Transform(curve_wide, curve_narrow),
            Write(label_large),
            label_small.animate.set_fill(opacity=0.3)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # "This relationship follows the predictable Standard Error formula."
        formula = MathTex(
            r"\text{Standard Error}", "=", r"\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}",
            color="#FFFF00"
        )
        self.place_in_area(formula, "A2", "A5", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # "Precision grows as the square root of sample size."
        # Highlight the \sqrt{n} part within the fraction of formula[2]
        sqrt_n_part = formula[2][2:] # Targeting the \sqrt{n} denominator part
        
        # Show an even narrower curve to emphasize precision growth
        curve_extra_narrow = get_bell_curve(0.25, "#00FFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(curve_extra_narrow, "E4")
        
        self.play(
            sqrt_n_part.animate.scale(1.4).set_color(WHITE),
            Flash(sqrt_n_part, color=WHITE, line_length=0.2)
        )
        self.play(
            Transform(curve_wide, curve_extra_narrow),
            sqrt_n_part.animate.scale(1/1.4).set_color("#FFFF00"),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(2)

class Section6Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Application: Why Does This Matter?", [
            "The CLT allows confident predictions about unknown populations.",
            "It's the secret foundation for polling and scientific research.",
            "Order emerges from chaos, making the unpredictable predictable."
        ])
        
        # Colors
        color_line1 = YELLOW
        color_line2 = BLUE
        color_line3 = RED
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(color_line1)
        
        # Elevator visual: A simple frame in the middle-right
        elevator_frame = Rectangle(width=3, height=4, color=LIGHT_GREY)
        self.place_in_area(elevator_frame, 'B2', 'E4')
        
        # Max Weight line at the top of the elevator
        max_y = self.grid['B2'][1] - 0.2
        max_weight_line = Line(
            start=[self.grid['B2'][0], max_y, 0],
            end=[self.grid['B4'][0], max_y, 0],
            color=color_line3
        )
        max_weight_label = Text("Max Weight", font_size=18, color=color_line3)
        self.place_at_grid(max_weight_label, 'B5', scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(Create(elevator_frame))
        self.play(Create(max_weight_line), Write(max_weight_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(color_line1) # Using Yellow for active line
        
        # Bell curve representing group weight (CLT)
        # We'll rotate it to show 'weight' on the Y axis as it 'fills' the elevator
        mu = self.grid['D3'][1]
        sigma = 0.5
        
        def vertical_pdf_func(y):
            # x = offset + peak * exp(...)
            return self.grid['C2'][0] + 1.5 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((y - mu) / sigma)**2)

        curve = ParametricFunction(
            lambda t: np.array([vertical_pdf_func(t), t, 0]),
            t_range=[self.grid['E3'][1] + 0.2, max_y + 0.4],
            color=color_line2
        )
        
        curve_label = Text("Weight Distribution", font_size=18, color=color_line2)
        self.place_at_grid(curve_label, 'D5', scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(Create(curve), Write(curve_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(color_line1)
        
        # Shade the tiny area beyond the 'Max Weight' (y > max_y)
        # We create a polygon for the tail
        tail_points = []
        # Sample points from the curve that are above the line
        for t in np.linspace(max_y, max_y + 0.4, 20):
            tail_points.append(np.array([vertical_pdf_func(t), t, 0]))
        
        # Close the polygon along the max weight line
        tail_points.append(np.array([self.grid['C2'][0], max_y + 0.4, 0]))
        tail_points.append(np.array([self.grid['C2'][0], max_y, 0]))
        
        shade_area = Polygon(*tail_points, color=color_line3, fill_opacity=0.5, stroke_width=0)
        
        risk_label = Text("Risk", font_size=18, color=color_line3)
        self.place_at_grid(risk_label, 'A4', scale_factor=0.8)

        self.play(FadeIn(shade_area), Write(risk_label))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Magic of the Central Limit Theorem: Order from Chaos
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students or introductory statistics learners

sections.title: The Hook: The Mystery of the Monster Forest
sections.content: Introduce the concept of 'unpredictable' data. Visualize a forest filled with monsters of wildly different heights—some tiny like squirrels, others giant like redwood trees. Their height distribution is messy and non-normal (skewed or multimodal).
sections.example: Imagine 'Zog' the data scientist monster. He looks at his messy forest map and wonders: 'How can I predict the average height of my neighbors if the data is so chaotic?'

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Populations vs. Samples
sections.content: Define the 'Population' (all monsters) and 'Sample' (a small group picked at random). Introduce the Mean (μ) and Standard Deviation (σ). Use a visual gauge to show these parameters for the whole forest.
sections.example: A visual animation showing Zog grabbing a net and catching 5 random monsters. This small group is a 'Sample,' and their average height is a 'Sample Mean' (x̄).

sections.title: The Experiment: The Power of Repetition
sections.content: Explain the process of repeated sampling. We don't just take one sample; we take thousands. Introduce the 'Sampling Distribution of the Mean.' Visual: A conveyor belt of monster groups being weighed and their averages recorded.
sections.example: Zog builds a robot that catches 30 monsters at a time, calculates their average height, drops a marble into a jar representing that average, and repeats this 1,000 times.

sections.title: The Core Revelation: The Bell Curve Emerges
sections.content: This is the 'Aha!' moment. Regardless of the original forest's messy distribution, the jar of marbles (sample means) begins to form a perfect, symmetrical Bell Curve (Normal Distribution). Emphasize the 'n ≥ 30' rule.
sections.example: An animation showing the messy forest histogram on the left and the beautiful, smooth bell curve forming on the right as the robot finishes its 1,000th sample.

sections.title: The Mathematical Logic: Mean and Spread
sections.content: Explain the two rules of the CLT: 1. The center of the bell curve is the same as the population mean (μ). 2. The curve gets narrower as the sample size (n) increases, following the formula: Standard Error = σ / √n.
sections.example: Show two bell curves: one where Zog catches 5 monsters at a time (wide curve), and one where he catches 100 at a time (very skinny, precise curve). This proves larger samples lead to less 'luck of the draw' error.

sections.title: Application: Why Does This Matter?
sections.content: Conclude by explaining that the CLT allows us to make confident predictions about a population even when we don't know its shape. It's the foundation for polling, quality control, and scientific research.
sections.example: Zog uses the bell curve to design an elevator for the monsters. Because of the CLT, he knows exactly how likely it is that a group of 30 monsters will exceed the weight limit, ensuring the elevator is safe even if he doesn't know every monster's exact weight.
